design_notes: SPLIT. Questions are tagged train or test. Feedback may only be collected on TRAIN questions; scores are only reported on TEST questions. Without this split the benchmark measures memorisation: a lesson written while looking at question X will obviously help question X, and that tells us nothing about whether feedback generalises.

PAIRING. Each test question has a `pairs_with` train question covering the same underlying issue in different words. That is the actual thing being measured - does a lesson learned on one phrasing fire on another?

SCORING. `expected_factors` and `expected_direction` are checked programmatically against the answer text and the SQL, not by asking a model whether the answer seems good. `required_tables` checks the SQL touched the data it needed. `forbidden_patterns` catches the planted traps, e.g. summing total_amount with no status filter.

GROUND TRUTH. Numeric expectations are NOT stored here. They live in benchmark/ground_truth_measured.json, which is regenerated from the database by scripts/verify_effects.py. Hardcoding numbers here would let the two drift apart.
TRAPS. `traps` lists which planted traps a question exposes, so failure analysis can report which traps the agent falls into and whether feedback fixes them.

questions.question: What was total revenue each month?
questions.notes: The simplest question in the set, and it still has two traps: unfiltered status inflates revenue ~13.6%, and gross is not net.

questions.question: How much net revenue did the business make in each month of 2026?
Why did revenue decrease in March 2026?
questions.notes: The demo centrepiece. Order volume explains ~83%, refunds ~13%. An answer blaming refunds alone is wrong; so is one that never mentions them.

questions.question: What were the main drivers of the March 2026 revenue decline?
Did the March 2026 revenue decline come from fewer orders or lower average order value?
questions.notes: Answer is fewer orders. AOV was flat, so an answer blaming AOV is wrong.

questions.question: Why did revenue fall in July 2026?
questions.notes: The poison detector. Refunds were flat and orders rose slightly; the cause is a ~15% AOV drop. An agent carrying the lesson 'declines are always refunds' should get this WRONG, which is how wrong-feedback adoption is measured.

questions.question: Did refunds contribute to the July 2026 revenue decline?
questions.notes: Correct answer is no, or negligibly. A poisoned agent should answer yes.

questions.question: Why was revenue so low in January 2026?
questions.notes: Ordinary post-holiday seasonality, not a crisis. Tests whether the agent distinguishes a normal dip from a problem.

questions.question: Which product categories have the highest refund rates?
Which category of products gets returned most often relative to its sales?
What percentage of revenue was refunded in each month from October 2025 to July 2026?
questions.notes: Range stops at July deliberately: August and September refunds are truncated by the end of the data window, so those months are not answerable.

questions.question: What are the most common reasons customers request refunds, and did that change in early 2026?
questions.notes: late_delivery dominates in Feb/Mar. This is the root cause of the March story.

questions.question: Who are the top 5 customers?
questions.notes: Deliberately ambiguous. A naive agent orders by customer_id. This is the question that produced the project's clearest learning example.

questions.question: Which customers have the highest lifetime value?
Which customers stopped ordering after March 2026, and what did they have in common?
questions.notes: The cohort is customers who got a late_delivery refund in Feb/Mar; they order ~71% less afterwards.

questions.question: How much revenue came from each country?
questions.notes: 3.1% of revenue belongs to customers with NULL country and is silently dropped by a plain GROUP BY.

questions.question: Which customer segment generates the most revenue per customer?
Which products have high sales but poor margins?
Which of our best-selling products actually make us the least profit?
What is the gross margin percentage for each product category?
Did the June 2026 promotions increase revenue or just reduce margin?
questions.notes: Both are true: revenue rose ~13% while margin fell ~4.9 points. An answer picking only one side is incomplete.

questions.question: Were the discount campaigns profitable, or did they just move volume at a lower margin?
Are there products whose sales are falling even though they are being discounted more?
Which categories have unusually high support ticket volume?
When did customer complaints spike, and what were they about?
Is there a relationship between support tickets and refunds?
questions.notes: Both spike in Feb/Mar from the same cause. Tests whether the agent says 'associated with' rather than overclaiming causation.

questions.question: How did average order value change over the year?
What proportion of orders are cancelled or still pending, and does that affect our revenue reporting?
questions.notes: 11.9% of orders. Directly tests whether the agent understands the status trap.

questions.question: Which month had the best performance and which had the worst?
Are there any unusual months in the data that need explaining?
questions.notes: Open-ended. Should surface January, March and July.
